title: Degenerated differential pair
description: A source-degenerated differential pair: a resistor $R_s$ in each source lifts the linear input range and improves offset at the cost of transconductance. The effective transconductance is $G_m = g_m/(1 + (g_m + g_{mb})*R_s)$; the degeneration factor $n_{deg} = 1 + (g_m + g_{mb})*R_s$ divides GBW and the input offset while the ~1-decade linear range extends to about $V^* + (I_{tail}/2)*R_s$. The two resistors meet at the tail node, and the tail is drawn: a diode-connected bias reference carries the programmed $I_{tail}$, the tail device sits on that reference's gate at that reference's width with the tail node as its drain, and each side of the pair carries half of what the tail delivers there. Entered from the COMMON MODE: the tail node $V_{tail}$ is the one free bias variable, solved by a design constraint so that the produced $CM_{in} = V_s + V_{GS}$ equals $CM_{dc}$. No gate is a port: the two inputs are held at $CM_{dc}$, and the two drains at $V_{out,dc}$, the level the undrawn load sets. The device's source node sits one resistor drop above the tail node, $V_s = V_{tail} + I_D*R_s$ — its FULL elevation above the bulk, tail lift and resistor drop together — and both bias coordinates follow from it ($v_{sb} = V_s$, $v_{ds} = V_{out} - V_s$), so the body effect is charged in full rather than only the resistor's few tens of millivolts. The resistor drop comes out of the tail device's drain-source voltage, so the low end of the common-mode range is where that device leaves saturation, and a check says so. Degeneration also raises each device's output resistance, to $r_o (1 + (g_m + g_{mb}) R_s) + R_s$, and the output resistance and the gain into the estimated load conductance count it.

params.name: Av_target
params.note: gain target AFTER degeneration: n_deg divides the raw gm, so this is what is left once the linear range is bought

params.name: GBW_target
params.note: bandwidth target after degeneration, same trade as the gain target

params.name: SR_target
params.note: slew-rate target: the tail current into the 2 pF load; 5 V/us moves a 0.5 V step in 100 ns, the range of a low-power transconductor at a 20 uA-class tail. An example, to be replaced with the design's own spec

params.name: linrange_target
params.note: required single-ended linear input range (differential is roughly twice this)

params.name: vn_target
params.note: input-referred thermal density budget, set above the 32.5 nV/rtHz floor measured on a sky130 tt realization of this pair rather than above the gamma-model estimate — a budget that only clears the model is not a budget. The degeneration resistor's own 4kT*R_s is the linearity price: at the default 12 kOhm it is most of the power, and the equation, reading the devices' own noise from a sky130 tt table, lands near 32.5 nV/rtHz

params.name: vos_target
params.note: input offset budget, 1 sigma

params.name: gds_load_est
params.note: conductance loading each drain; R_L = 1/gds_load_est

params.name: CM_lo
params.note: input CM range the application presents, low end — checked exactly by the cm-lo range end at every evaluation (the sweep put the widest closing range at 1.03-1.31 V on sky130 tt at the shipped choices). The low end is where the tail node falls under about 0.2 V: the tail device then delivers less, the resistor drop shrinks, and the linear-range target is the first to go. The range end checks the ENDPOINT; the interior is the sweep's to show

params.name: CM_hi
params.note: input CM range the application presents, high end — its ENDPOINT checked by the cm-hi range end the same way

params.name: CM_dc
params.note: the input common mode the application presents. The engine places the tail node so the sheet sits exactly here; sweep it to trace the common-mode axis

params.name: V_out_dc
params.note: drain DC level; sets the input device vds. Whatever terminates the drains sets it (a mirror diode drop, a resistor drop, a folded-cascode source), and that load is not on this sheet: only its conductance, gds_load_est, is

params.name: V_tail
params.note: the tail node — the tail device's drain, where the two degeneration resistors meet. Solved rather than set: searched between min and max (the range it is searched in, not slider bounds) until the produced common mode equals CM_dc. The input device's source sits one resistor drop above it. The range reaches below the tail device's saturation voltage on purpose: a common mode that leaves the tail too little drain-source voltage then lands and fails the tail device's saturation check, where a higher floor would leave the question unanswered

params.name: avt
params.note: Pelgrom A_VT

params.name: abeta
params.note: Pelgrom A_beta

params.name: I_tail
params.note: the current the bias reference is programmed to — the one current on this sheet that is typed. The tail device mirrors it 1:1 through the shared gate and delivers it less the mirror's drain-voltage error (the tail node normally sits below the reference's diode drop); the resistor drop, slew rate, linear range and supply current are computed from what is delivered, not from this number

params.name: R_s
params.note: per-side degeneration resistance; (gm + gmb)*R_s sets the linearization and offset improvement

params.name: gm_id_in
params.note: input-pair inversion; high gm/ID makes degeneration more effective (larger (gm + gmb)*R_s)

params.name: gm_id_tail
params.note: inversion level of the bias reference, which the tail device inherits through the shared gate: higher V* costs CM-low headroom. Set as weak as the pair's, because the resistor drop is taken out of the tail device's drain-source voltage

params.name: L_in
params.note: input-pair length. Long, because the gain is taken into a fixed load conductance and the degeneration has already divided the transconductance: the device's own output conductance has to stay well under the load's for the gain target to hold

params.name: L_tail
params.note: length of the bias reference and of the tail device, which mirror at one length: longer shrinks the mirror's drain-voltage error

doc.title: Tail current source
doc.description: The tail device, on the bias reference's gate at the reference's width: a 1:1 mirror of the programmed current, with the tail node as its drain-source voltage. Its current is read off the table rather than typed — the reference sits at its own diode drop and this device at $V_{tail}$, so it delivers the programmed current scaled by what that difference in $V_{DS}$ does through its $g_{ds}$. It leaves saturation when $V_{tail}$ falls below its own $V_{dsat}$, which is what sets the low end of the usable common-mode range.

params.name: W_t
params.note: the bias reference's width — a 1:1 copy

params.name: vgs_t
params.note: the bias reference's gate voltage — the gate wire the two share

params.name: vds_t
params.note: the tail node

doc.title: Input-pair device (degenerated)
doc.description: Half-circuit input device, carrying half of what the tail delivers, with R_s between its source and the tail node. Its source node V_s sits that current's drop across R_s above the tail node: vsb = V_s (the FULL elevation above the bulk, not just the resistor lift) and vds = V_out_dc - V_s.

params.name: vsb_i
params.note: the source node — the device's full elevation above the bulk

equations.name: V_s
equations.note: the input device's source node — its full elevation above the bulk: the tail node plus the drop the device's own current makes across its resistor. It is the device's body bias, and its drain-source voltage is what is left between the drain level and this node

equations.name: CM_in
equations.note: the input common mode this bias produces — an OUTPUT here, not a setting; rises monotonically with the tail node, so the design constraint is a well-posed one-unknown search

equations.name: n_deg
equations.note: degeneration factor; Gm, GBW, and vos all scale by 1/n_deg. The source node carries the source-body generator's current through the same resistor, so gmb degenerates alongside gm — on a sky130 tt realization of this pair that takes the factor from 2.68 to 3.07 and lines Gm_eff and GBW up with the measured transfer instead of leaving them ~11% high. The device's own gds returns to the source node too, but at these impedances it is worth under 1% of the factor and is left out

equations.name: Rout
equations.note: the resistance this stage presents at its output: the input device's output resistance as its source resistor raises it, ro*(1 + (gm + gmb)*R_s) + R_s, which is ro*n_deg + R_s, in parallel with the estimated load conductance. A current change at the drain moves the source by R_s times it, and the device answers through gm + gmb because its body stays at ground. Worked from the simulated devices this gives the simulated output resistance exactly; the device's bare ro read it 18 % low. The gain assumes a capacitive load, so nothing here models a resistive one; this equation is what a composing parent checks its own loading against

equations.name: Av
equations.note: the degenerated transconductance into the degeneration-boosted device resistance in parallel with the estimated load

equations.name: SR
equations.note: the whole tail current steered into the load — the current the tail device delivers, not the number the reference is programmed to

equations.name: linrange
equations.note: single-ended linear range ~ V* + I*R_s (V* = 2/(gm/ID)), with I the current the input device carries — half of what the tail delivers

equations.name: vos_undeg
equations.note: the un-degenerated Pelgrom offset of the input pair

equations.name: vos
equations.note: degeneration divides the offset by n_deg (the gm-mismatch term is linearized away)

equations.name: vn_in
equations.note: device density plus the degeneration resistor's 4kT*R_s, both sides of the pair (estimate). The resistor's noise is a voltage in series with the source, and the source drives the channel through gm + gmb, so it refers to the gate through (gm + gmb)/gm, not 1. The device's own term is its gate-referred density as it stands

equations.name: tail_headroom
equations.note: how far the tail node sits above the tail device's saturation voltage — exact here, because the tail node is the variable rather than something inferred from a common mode

equations.name: cgg_in
equations.note: estimate: the capacitance one input terminal presents — the gate capacitance of a single input device. Gate capacitance only, because the Miller term needs the gate-drain fraction and these tables do not carry it, so a driving stage sees more than this. No check reads it

equations.name: I_q
equations.note: estimate: quiescent supply current — the current the tail device delivers is the only branch these equations model, since the load is entered as a conductance rather than sized as a branch. The reference branch that programs the tail is shared bias infrastructure, typically one reference feeding several stages, and is not counted here. The datasheet line for comparing designs; no check reads it

checks.note: degeneration must extend the linear range to the target

reads each device's thermal noise from the table where the table carries it, and the gamma = 1 estimate where it does not; it stays advisory because a sheet cannot know which table it will be evaluated on, and the simulator owns noise sign-off
trips when the source node is pushed so high the device runs out of drain-source voltage at the drain DC level
the common mode this bias produces has to sit inside the range the application presents
paired with cm-not-below; the cm-lo/cm-hi range ends check the held design at the ENDS of the range, and the CM_dc sweep shows the whole landscape

operatingRange.name: cm-lo
operatingRange.note: the claimed low end, checked exactly: the whole sheet re-evaluates at CM_dc = CM_lo on the design this run produced — its own tail-node solve over its full range, every device held at the geometry it was sized to — and every physical and spec check must hold there

operatingRange.name: cm-hi
operatingRange.note: the claimed high end, checked the same way. The range ends check the ENDPOINTS; the CM_dc sweep remains the authority on the full landscape
